clue.text: Half inclined to stay away, the fly one!

definitions.text: Half inclined to stay away, the fly one!

parts.words: Half inclined to stay away, the fly one
parts.note: in rugby the fly-half is also called by a name meaning aloof, so a half-back 'inclined to stay away' is the fly one

explanation.surface: Someone only half minded to keep their distance, and a sly one at that.
explanation.walkthrough: In rugby the fly-half, the back who receives the ball from the scrum-half, is also called the stand-off half; 'stand-off' also means aloof, which is what 'inclined to stay away' plays on.
explanation.definitionFit: Rugby union uses both names for the same back-line position, the playmaker standing off from the scrum.

clue.text: Spray the grapes

annotationWithheld.why: 'Spray the grapes': SPARGE is an anagram of 'grapes', but no word indicates it; 'Spray' would have to be both definition and anagram indicator

clue.text: Look, going in a covered wagon to' Arthur's place

indicators.note: the interjection is said to go into the vehicle, so it sits inside that word

parts.note: a van is a covered vehicle for goods
lo is an old word meaning look or behold

explanation.surface: A traveller climbs into a covered wagon bound for King Arthur's home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going in' puts LO inside VAN, giving VALON after the A.
explanation.definitionFit: In legend the island of Avalon is where the wounded King Arthur was carried after his last battle.

clue.text: A shelved medical assistant

definitions.meaning: a shelved one: a kitchen cabinet with open shelves above for plates
an assistant who dresses wounds, especially for a surgeon

explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a sideboard with plate shelves and a hospital helper who applies bandages for the surgeon.

clue.text: First showing of her entering No. 10 ?

definitions.text: First showing of her entering No. 10 ?

parts.words: First showing of her entering No. 10
parts.note: a woman prime minister would be a feminine premier with an added E, and her arrival at Downing Street a first showing

explanation.surface: The debut of a woman moving into 10 Downing Street, the British prime minister's residence.
explanation.walkthrough: No. 10 Downing Street is the British prime minister's home; a female premier is jokily given the feminine French ending -E, so 'her entering No. 10' suggests the feminine premier while 'First showing' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A cinema's opening-night screening of a new picture is its debut, the first public showing.

clue.text: About now Boreas has Gilpin's reputation

parts.note: re is Latin for concerning, about
taken as written
Boreas is the Greek god of the north wind, so N for north

explanation.surface: The north wind is now blowing about John Gilpin's good name.
explanation.walkthrough: William Cowper's comic poem begins 'John Gilpin was a citizen / Of credit and renown', so the poem gives Gilpin's reputation.
explanation.definitionFit: Fame and repute are the same thing; Cowper's line gives Gilpin credit and this.

clue.text: Overlooking the subject of a lover's ballad

definitions.text: Overlooking the subject of a lover's ballad

parts.words: Overlooking the subject of a lover's ballad
parts.note: a facial feature that sits over the eye, and in As You Like It the lover sighs a woeful ballad made to his mistress' one

explanation.surface: Someone ignoring the person a love song is written about.
explanation.walkthrough: In As You Like It Jaques describes the lover 'sighing like furnace, with a woeful ballad made to his mistress' eyebrow'; 'Overlooking' means sitting above the eye, not ignoring.
explanation.definitionFit: The arch of hair above each eye overlooks the eye itself.

clue.text: "Marry him ? The deuce !" cried Mistress Parr perhaps

definitions.text: "Marry him ? The deuce !" cried Mistress Parr perhaps

parts.words: Marry him ? The deuce !" cried Mistress Parr perhaps
parts.note: Catherine Parr married an aging Henry VIII, and a nickname for the devil, an exclamation like 'the deuce', also fits an elderly Henry

explanation.surface: A Tudor lady recoils at a proposal, swearing at the thought of the groom.
explanation.walkthrough: Catherine Parr was the sixth wife of Henry VIII, an elderly Harry by then; 'Old Harry' is also a name for the devil, which 'The deuce!' means as an oath.
explanation.definitionFit: Old Harry is a traditional nickname for Satan, and 'deuce' is a mild old word for the devil.

clue.text: Numbness of Rats ?

definitions.meaning: numbness is having no feeling, read as a lack of sense
'Rats!' is an exclamation dismissing something as rubbish

explanation.definitionFit: Read as non-sense the word means an absence of feeling; as one word it means rubbish, what 'Rats!' scornfully declares.

clue.text: Stuart or a Wilfer art associate

parts.note: ARA stands for Associate of the Royal Academy, an artists' honour
Bella Wilfer is the heroine of Dickens's Our Mutual Friend

explanation.surface: Choosing between a Stuart princess and a Dickens heroine, with a Royal Academy painter in tow.
explanation.walkthrough: Lady Arabella Stuart was a cousin of James I with a claim to the English throne; 'a Wilfer' is the Dickens heroine Bella, from Our Mutual Friend.
explanation.definitionFit: Lady Arabella Stuart, a Jacobean noblewoman, bore this first name.

clue.text: Female beak in North London college ?

parts.note: a hen is a female bird
beak is slang for a schoolmaster, here a college teacher, a don

explanation.surface: A woman magistrate sitting in a college in north London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beak' looks like a magistrate in British slang, but here it is the schoolmaster sense, a don. Hendon in north London is home to the Metropolitan Police training college.
explanation.definitionFit: The Metropolitan Police training college at Hendon is commonly known by the suburb's name.

clue.text: Gray grave ways

parts.note: Thomas Gray's Elegy says the routes to fame lead but to the grave

explanation.surface: Dull, solemn habits.
explanation.walkthrough: In Gray's 'Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard' a line runs 'The paths of glory lead but to the grave'; 'Gray' is the poet, not the colour.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase from Gray's Elegy names the routes to fame which, the poem says, end only in the grave.

clue.text: Town that makes lustre-work

parts.note: gloss is a shiny surface, lustre
op is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: A town whose trade is glazed lustreware.
explanation.walkthrough: Glossop is a town in Derbyshire.
explanation.definitionFit: Glossop is a market town on the edge of the Peak District.

clue.text: A city has antiquity to a certain extent

parts.note: Acre is an ancient port city in Israel
great age is antiquity

explanation.surface: An old city that is ancient up to a point.
explanation.definitionFit: The amount of land measured in acres is an area, a particular extent.

clue.text: Regiment adds colour to Forster's End

parts.note: green is a colour
E. M. Forster wrote the novel Howards End

explanation.surface: A regiment adds paint to the house in Forster's novel.
explanation.walkthrough: The Green Howards were a British infantry regiment from Yorkshire.
explanation.definitionFit: The Green Howards were a Yorkshire line infantry regiment of the British Army.

clue.text: Back to front in Surrey

parts.note: hind means at the back, as in hind legs
the head is the front, as of a queue

explanation.surface: Something turned the wrong way round somewhere in Surrey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back to front' looks like an instruction to reverse, but it is two pieces joined. Hindhead is a village in Surrey, a county south of London.
explanation.definitionFit: Hindhead is a hilltop village in the county of Surrey, so it is a place found there.

clue.text: Shropshire home of old style G.W.R. ?.

parts.note: OS is the abbreviation for Old Style, the calendar before 1752
the Great Western Railway, shortened to its Western Railway, written West. Ry.

explanation.surface: A Shropshire town that housed the old Great Western Railway works.
explanation.walkthrough: Oswestry, a Shropshire border town, was a railway centre; G.W.R. stands for Great Western Railway, abbreviated here as WEST RY.
explanation.definitionFit: Oswestry is a market town in Shropshire near the Welsh border.

clue.text: Eaters of bread-and-butter in Looking-glass Land, like the chameleon

definitions.text: Eaters of bread-and-butter in Looking-glass Land, like the chameleon

parts.words: Eaters of bread-and-butter in Looking-glass Land, like the chameleon
parts.note: in Through the Looking-Glass there is a Bread-and-butter-fly, a creature that the lizard named would eat

explanation.surface: Creatures in Lewis Carroll's mirror world who eat bread and butter, as a chameleon does.
explanation.walkthrough: Through the Looking-Glass has a Bread-and-butter-fly, so eaters of it eat flies, as the chameleon does.
explanation.definitionFit: Animals that feed on bugs are classed as such; the chameleon catches flies with its tongue.

clue.text: To do his job on stage may sound odious

definitions.text: To do his job on stage may sound odious

parts.words: To do his job on stage may sound odious
parts.note: the host's verb sounds like 'compare', and comparisons are proverbially odious

explanation.surface: Doing a performer's job on stage might seem a hateful task.
explanation.walkthrough: The verb for hosting a show sounds like 'compare', and the proverb says 'comparisons are odious'.
explanation.definitionFit: A master of ceremonies introduces the acts on stage; doing so is this verb.

clue.text: Town lovingly built in' the Adam style ?

definitions.text: Town lovingly built in' the Adam style ?

parts.words: Town lovingly built in' the Adam style
parts.note: split as the first woman's possessive plus a word for a pretence, the town's name suggests a loving imitation of Adam

explanation.surface: A town built with affection in the Neo-classical Adam architectural style.
explanation.walkthrough: The Adam style is an 18th-century architecture, but here Adam is the first man: Eve was built from his rib, so the town reads as EVE'S HAM. Evesham is a Worcestershire market town.
explanation.definitionFit: Evesham is a market town in Worcestershire in the Vale of Evesham.

clue.text: Obtained water abroad to eat

parts.note: gat is an old past tense of get, meaning obtained
eau is French for water

explanation.surface: Fetching water in a foreign country to have with a meal.
explanation.definitionFit: A rich cake is something to eat.

clue.text: Good, when the glass is going up

definitions.text: Good, when the glass is going up

parts.words: Good, when the glass is going up
parts.note: the toast 'Good ...!' is said as a drinking glass is raised

explanation.surface: Good news when the barometer is rising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the glass' looks like a barometer, but it is a drinking glass raised in the toast 'Good health!'.
explanation.definitionFit: Wellbeing is what a drinker wishes the company when raising a glass.

clue.text: He has, a fancy, to see me wrapped in melancholy

indicators.note: the pronoun is enclosed by the word for gloom, so it goes inside

parts.note: drear is a poetic word for gloomy, melancholy
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone who has taken a liking finds himself wrapped in gloom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrapped in' puts ME inside DREAR. Someone who fancies things, an imaginer, is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A fantasist is someone given to flights of fancy.

clue.text: British nonpareil's French pomegranate

definitions.meaning: the song The British Grenadiers says none can compare with the British Grenadier, and the bomb is his weapon
the French word for the fruit pomegranate

explanation.definitionFit: The French word for pomegranate gave English its name for a hand bomb, the weapon of the Grenadier whom the song ranks beyond compare.

clue.text: Admittedly I'm dished

parts.note: a word that means both the right of admission and a course served at dinner

explanation.surface: Someone conceding that they are ruined.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dished' looks like ruined, but means served as a dish; 'Admittedly' points to the other sense, right of entry.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means a right of admittance and also a dish served at a meal.

clue.text: Report on twins' born on Clydeside ?

definitions.text: Report on twins' born on Clydeside

parts.words: Report on twins' born on Clydeside
parts.note: a bulletin after a twin birth would say the pair are healthy, which names a Clydeside town

explanation.surface: A bulletin about twins delivered on the River Clyde in Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: The news of a twin birth, 'both well', is the name of Bothwell, a town on the Clyde in Lanarkshire.
explanation.definitionFit: Bothwell is a town on the River Clyde near Glasgow.

clue.text: This poet's environment was not Wordsworth's idea of Milton's

definitions.text: This poet's environment was not Wordsworth's idea of Milton's

parts.words: This poet's environment was not Wordsworth's idea of Milton's
parts.note: Wordsworth called England a fen of stagnant waters in his sonnet to Milton; the opposite, an arid lair, gives this poet

explanation.surface: A poet whose surroundings were nothing like what Wordsworth imagined for Milton.
explanation.walkthrough: In 'London, 1802' Wordsworth says England 'is a fen of stagnant waters'; the opposite of a wet fen is a DRY DEN, the name of the poet John Dryden.
explanation.definitionFit: John Dryden was the English poet laureate of the Restoration.

clue.text: Berwickshire's facial! characteristics

parts.note: the eye is a feature of the face
the mouth is another feature of the face

explanation.surface: The typical faces of people from the Scottish county of Berwickshire.
explanation.walkthrough: Eyemouth is a fishing town in Berwickshire, a county in south-east Scotland; 'Berwickshire's' stands for a town there.
explanation.definitionFit: Eyemouth is a fishing port on the Berwickshire coast, so it belongs to that county.
